articles.title: Paramount Skydance's $110 billion Warner Bros. Discovery takeover heads toward a March trial
articles.dek: A dozen state attorneys general are suing to block the deal even after the Justice Department cleared it, setting up a courtroom fight over one of media's largest-ever mergers.
articles.author: SOPHIA REYES | New York
body: Paramount Skydance's roughly $110 billion agreement to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, one of the largest media mergers ever proposed, remains tied up in court months after federal regulators signed off on it. The Justice Department cleared the deal in June, but twelve state attorneys general have sued to block it, arguing the combination would concentrate too much control over film, television and streaming in a single company. A trial date has been set for March 2, 2027.

The proposed deal, valued at $31.00 per share, would combine Paramount's television, film and streaming operations with Warner Bros. Discovery's stable of studios and cable networks, creating a company with an outsized share of scripted television production and one of the largest film libraries in the industry. Deal advisers say the merger is one of roughly twenty major acquisitions, worth a combined $600 billion, still waiting on final regulatory or court approval as of August.

Executives on both sides have continued to express confidence the deal will close, pointing to the federal clearance as evidence the combination does not run afoul of antitrust law. The states pursuing the lawsuit have countered that a merger of this scale deserves scrutiny beyond a single federal review, particularly given how much consumer entertainment spending would run through the combined company.

With the trial not scheduled until next spring, the companies face an extended stretch of uncertainty over integration planning, executive roles and programming strategy — all while continuing to operate as separate, competing businesses in the meantime.

articles.title: Union Pacific's $85 billion Norfolk Southern merger remains stalled in regulatory review
articles.dek: The proposed transcontinental rail combination has been held in abeyance by federal regulators since the spring, leaving one of the year's biggest industrial deals in limbo.
articles.author: SOPHIA REYES | New York
body: Union Pacific's proposed $85 billion acquisition of Norfolk Southern, which would create the first single railroad spanning the United States coast to coast, remains on hold at the Surface Transportation Board, the federal agency responsible for approving major rail mergers. The board placed the deal in abeyance in May, and as of August it has yet to set a firm timeline for resuming formal review.

The merger would combine Union Pacific's Western network with Norfolk Southern's Eastern lines, creating a single carrier able to move freight across the country without handing shipments off to a second railroad partway through the journey. Supporters argue the combination would speed shipping times and reduce costs for manufacturers, farmers and retailers who rely on rail freight. Shippers' groups and competing railroads have raised concerns about reduced competition on routes where the combined company would have little rival service.

The deal ranks among the largest pending mergers in any industry, trailing only a handful of transactions such as the proposed Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery combination in overall size. Because rail mergers of this scale require the Surface Transportation Board's approval rather than a standard antitrust review, the process tends to move more slowly and involves a more extensive public comment period than typical corporate acquisitions.

Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern have said they still expect the deal to close, though neither company has offered a revised timeline. Analysts tracking the merger say the board's approach here could shape whether other long-discussed rail consolidations move forward in the coming years.

articles.title: Prologis to acquire UK's Segro in $18.8 billion logistics real estate deal
articles.dek: The acquisition expands the world's largest warehouse landlord deeper into European industrial property as e-commerce and supply-chain shifts keep reshaping demand for logistics space.
articles.author: SOPHIA REYES | New York
body: Prologis, the largest owner of warehouse and logistics real estate in the world, agreed in August to acquire UK-based Segro in a transaction valued at approximately $18.8 billion, extending the American company's footprint into European industrial and warehouse property.

The deal brings together Prologis's global logistics network with Segro's portfolio of distribution centers and industrial parks concentrated in the United Kingdom and continental Europe, giving the combined company a larger base from which to serve retailers, manufacturers and logistics firms that lease large-scale warehouse space near ports, highways and population centers.

Prologis said the acquisition supports its long-term push to expand across logistics, energy infrastructure and digital infrastructure — a strategy that has taken on new urgency as data centers and e-commerce fulfillment operations compete for many of the same large industrial sites. Segro shareholders will need to approve the deal before it can close.

The transaction is among the largest real estate deals announced this year and reflects continued consolidation among warehouse landlords as companies seek scale to negotiate with large corporate tenants and fund the kind of automation and energy upgrades increasingly demanded by logistics customers.

articles.title: Tech layoffs mount through 2026 as Zillow, Apple and Microsoft all cut jobs
articles.dek: Job cuts across the technology sector have already topped last year's total, with companies pointing to cost discipline, restructuring and the growing use of AI in day-to-day operations.
articles.author: SOPHIA REYES | New York
body: The wave of technology-sector layoffs that has defined 2026 shows little sign of slowing. By early August, the number of tech workers laid off this year had already surpassed the total for all of 2025, according to data compiled by the layoff-tracking site Layoffs.fyi, and additional rounds of cuts continued through the month.

Real estate platform Zillow said in early August it would lay off just over 500 employees, with chief executive Jeremy Wacksman describing the move as part of an effort to maintain "a disciplined cost structure" and put the right people in the right roles. Later in the month, Apple cut more than 60 employees from its Vision Pro team along with additional staff from its Siri organization — notable in part because Apple rarely announces layoffs of any size. Microsoft has attributed a reduction of 4,800 positions in part to how artificial intelligence is changing the way work gets done, even as the company said the eliminated roles were not being directly replaced by AI systems.

Industry analysts point to several overlapping causes: companies recalibrating headcount after pandemic-era hiring surges, macroeconomic caution, and a broad push to fold AI tools into operations in ways that reduce demand for certain roles, particularly in content moderation, customer support and some engineering functions. At the same time, many of the same companies continue hiring for AI-specific roles, including machine learning engineering and AI safety positions.

For workers, the practical effect has been a tighter and more unpredictable job market in a sector that spent much of the previous decade adding staff aggressively. Outplacement firms say severance packages and internal transfer opportunities have varied widely by company, with larger firms generally offering more generous transition support than smaller platforms.

articles.title: Aon to acquire USI Insurance Services from KKR in $17 billion deal
articles.dek: The transaction expands Aon's reach into the fast-growing middle-market insurance segment and marks a major private equity exit for KKR.
articles.author: SOPHIA REYES | New York
body: Insurance broker Aon announced a $17 billion agreement in August to acquire USI Insurance Services from private equity firm KKR, a deal that expands Aon's presence in the middle-market insurance business serving small and mid-sized companies.

USI, which provides insurance brokerage and consulting services to businesses across the United States, has grown substantially under KKR's ownership. The sale represents one of the private equity firm's largest exits of the year and comes as insurance brokerages have drawn steady interest from both strategic buyers and investment firms seeking stable, fee-based revenue streams.

For Aon, the acquisition adds scale in a segment of the insurance market that has historically been served by a fragmented mix of regional and independent brokers. Industry analysts have described the U.S. middle-market insurance segment as one of the faster-growing corners of the industry, driven by demand from mid-sized employers for more sophisticated risk management and benefits consulting.

The deal is one of several large insurance-sector transactions announced this year, as brokers and carriers alike pursue consolidation to spread technology costs and compete for larger corporate accounts. Completion of the acquisition remains subject to customary regulatory approvals.

articles.title: Walmart, Target and Home Depot earnings point to a resilient but price-conscious shopper
articles.dek: Walmart posted its weakest sales growth in more than six years, while Target and Home Depot both reported gains, as retailers described customers trading down without pulling back entirely.
articles.author: SOPHIA REYES | New York
body: A closely watched week of retail earnings gave Wall Street a fresh read on the American consumer, as Home Depot, Target and Walmart each reported quarterly results showing shoppers still spending — but increasingly focused on price.

Walmart, which reported Thursday, posted its weakest sales growth in more than six years, a slowdown the company attributed primarily to softness in its pharmacy business rather than a broader pullback in shopping. Target and Home Depot, which reported earlier in the week, both posted sales gains and described resilient customers who continue to spend when they find the right product at the right price.

The results followed a Commerce Department report showing that Americans unexpectedly cut back on retail spending in July by the largest amount in more than a year, raising questions about whether the pullback would carry into the retailers' next quarterly results. Executives at all three companies said elevated fuel costs and broader inflation pressures have made shoppers more deliberate, prompting some to trade down to cheaper private-label products or delay discretionary purchases.

Target's results came under new chief executive Michael Fiddelke, a 20-year company veteran who took over in February and has been working to stabilize sales after a stretch of underperformance relative to rivals. Analysts said the retail sector's mixed but broadly steady results suggested consumer spending was slowing rather than breaking down, a distinction likely to factor into the Federal Reserve's interest-rate deliberations later in September.
